discriminative_rationale: A genuine single-phase fault raises the differential on exactly one pair while the remaining pairs keep balanced, proportionate amplitudes -- the localisation a real physical fault produces.

Genuine fault currents remain sample-to-sample continuous because circuit inductance opposes instantaneous change; moderate roughness alongside a real differential indicates a physical transient rather than substituted samples.

Inductance prevents instantaneous current change, so elevated normalised sample-to-sample variation indicates splice points where injected values replaced measured ones. Measured: attack windows show roughly twice the roughness of fault windows.

A physical transformer event preserves proportionate amplitude relationships across all six measured channels. An adversary altering a subset of reported values breaks those relationships, producing amplitude dispersion no single physical event explains. Strongest single discriminator measured on this dataset.

Simultaneous elevated differential on two or more pairs is inconsistent with the localised single-phase faults this relay observes, and indicates coordinated manipulation of multiple measurement channels.

Input and output currents of one differential pair retain comparable magnitudes through a genuine event. A large mismatch within a pair suggests one side's reported values were altered independently of the other.
During an internal fault the C‑pair differential stays well below the restraint current, a region never reached by attacks in the hard‑event set.
A genuine internal fault appears as a single hot pair; events with no hot pair are unlikely to be attack‑driven manipulations.
Abrupt sample‑to‑sample jumps in phase A are unlikely in physical phenomena but are common when adversaries tamper with measurement streams.
